name: Avebury, Silbury Hill, Maiden Castle and the Uffington White Horse
about: Four earthwork sites whose ground comes from the Environment Agency's 1 m LiDAR. The facts here are what the LiDAR cannot give: what each is, its dates and phases, what was lost or added, the structures on it (stones, posts, gates, timber and stone faces of ramparts, the temple), and astronomical claims. avebury.name: Avebury henge and stone circles
avebury.about: A Late Neolithic henge in Wiltshire: a bank with an internal ditch, broken by four causewayed entrances (north, east, south, west), enclosing the largest stone circle in Britain (originally about 98, or 98-105, sarsens set just inside the ditch) and two inner circles, the Northern (about 27 stones, with the three-sided Cove at its centre) and the Southern (29 stones round the Obelisk, a stone about 5.5-6.4 m tall, with the small 'Z-feature' setting beside it, now argued to be part of a 30 m square). The earthwork seen today was built about 2580-2470 cal BC over a smaller first bank; the outer circle a little later; the Cove may be as early as 3000 cal BC. Villagers buried many stones from the early 14th century (the 'barber-surgeon' was crushed by one) and broke up most of the rest by fire and water in the late 17th-18th centuries; the Obelisk went after 1725. Alexander Keiller excavated the West Kennet Avenue (1934-35) and the NW (1937), SW (1938) and SE (1939) sectors, re-erected the buried and fallen stones he found in their own stone-holes (the western half of the outer circle and the Southern Inner Circle) and set concrete pillars on the holes of destroyed stones; the eastern half was never excavated and several stones still lie buried there (2003 survey). Today about 30 stones of the outer circle are visible and 16 more positions are marked by concrete pillars (Wessex Archaeology); of the Northern Inner Circle two stand and two lie; of the Cove two stones stand (straightened in 2003). The earthwork and its present heights come from the EA LiDAR; quotes below give the original depths.

silbury.name: Silbury Hill
silbury.about: The largest prehistoric artificial mound in Europe, 1.6 km south of Avebury: a chalk mound about 30-31 m high (Wikipedia: 39.3 m) and 160-167 m across at the base, with a flat top about 30 m across and a step or terrace a few metres below it, built in many stages over 50-150 years from about 2490-2450 cal BC: a small gravel mound, a stake ring 16 m across filled with dark soils and turf, a 35 m mound about 5 m high, then a 100 m ditched enclosure, then the chalk mound itself quarried from a great ditch round it, which widens on the west into a rectangular 'tank' that floods in winter. Its base has straight construction lines (up to nine). The summit was probably flattened in the early medieval period for a defensive structure. A Roman settlement lay round its foot and the Roman road (A4) swerves round it. Shafts and tunnels were dug in 1776 (Drax, from the top), 1849 (Merewether) and 1968-70 (Atkinson); a crater opened on the summit in 2000 and in 2007-08 English Heritage refilled all known voids with 1,465 tonnes of chalk. Nothing stands on it; the shape now is the LiDAR's. Originally the chalk was white.

maiden_castle.name: Maiden Castle, Dorset
maiden_castle.about: One of the largest Iron Age hillforts in Europe, on a saddle-backed chalk hill 2.6 km south-west of Dorchester with two knolls. Before the fort: an Early Neolithic causewayed enclosure of two interrupted ditches on the eastern knoll (about 3800-3400 BC), then a bank barrow 546 m (1,790 ft) long and 18 m (60 ft) wide between flanking ditches, nearly ploughed out; Bronze Age round barrows. The first hillfort (about 600 BC) followed the line of the Neolithic enclosure: a single rampart and V-shaped ditch round 6.4 ha (16 acres) of the eastern knoll, with a north-west entrance and a double east entrance. About 450 BC it was extended west over Hog Hill to 19 ha (47 acres) and given more ramparts: four ramparts and three ditches on the south, three ramparts on the steeper north; inner rampart about 2 km round; complex outworks at the eastern and western double entrances; at the west end of the old fort its western rampart and gate survive as earthworks inside. Inner rampart timber-revetted early, later chalk dump with a limestone wall. Wheeler excavated in 1934-37 (the 'war cemetery' at the eastern entrance); Sharples in 1985-86. A Romano-British temple (a cella with an ambulatory, east door), a priest's house and a round shrine were built about AD 370 in the eastern half, with a stone gateway in the east entrance. A square dew-pond of the 1860s is in the middle. The earthworks come from the EA LiDAR; quotes give the original heights where they differ.

uffington.name: Uffington White Horse, Uffington Castle and Dragon Hill
uffington.about: The White Horse is Britain's oldest chalk hill figure, about 110 m long, near the top of the steep north-west-facing slope above the dry valley called the Manger, on the Berkshire Downs in Oxfordshire; its head points up the hill (south-west) and its body curves round the valley side towards Dragon Hill. It is not a plain cut in the turf: first made by exposing the bedrock, it was kept by trenches packed with rammed or puddled chalk, renewed again and again, so seven or eight surfaces lie one on another; it has narrowed slightly (the body about 1 m, a hind leg 0.6 m) and its slope has dropped by about 10 degrees; a concrete kerb now holds the belly edge. OSL dates on the hillwash put the first horse at 1380-550 BC (68%) or 1740-210 BC (95%), late Bronze Age or early Iron Age. Scoured by local people every seven years until 1857 (last by the landlord in 1892), covered in the Second World War, restored 1951-53, re-chalked by the National Trust's volunteers (since 2009); found shrinking up to 40% and widened from 2024. Above it, Uffington Castle, an early Iron Age hillfort (8th-7th century BC) of about 3.2-3.4 ha with a single rampart and ditch and a counterscarp bank, an entrance on the west and a blocked one on the east: first a timber-framed box rampart with a double row of posts, then a chalk dump rampart with chalk and sarsen kerbs, the ditch recut. Below it, Dragon Hill, a natural chalk knoll with an artificially flattened circular top.

Its longest extent is 103 m at azimuth 5 degrees (derived), i.e. the mapped horse runs nearly north-south, which does not fit Pollard's NE-SW alignment or the 110 m length: probably a rough or misplaced trace; check against the LiDAR or aerial photographs before using it

gaps: Avebury per-stone list: which numbered stones stand, were re-erected in 1937-39, are concrete pillars or are destroyed is in Isobel Smith, Windmill Hill and Avebury (1965) and Ucko et al., Avebury Reconsidered (1991): neither is online. Keiller 1939 gives the NW and SW sectors in his own sector numbering (not Smith's); the SE sector (1939, Southern Inner Circle) and the West Kennet Avenue (Antiquity 1936, 10, 417-427) were not checked here. Count today: only Wessex Archaeology's round '30 visible + 16 concrete pillars'.
Avebury: no OSM stone has a number or tells stone from concrete pillar; matching the 84 outlines to Smith's numbers needs Smith's plan or a site visit / photographs.

Historic England list entries (Avebury 1008323, Silbury, Maiden Castle, Uffington) and research reports (Field 2002, The Investigation and Analytical Survey of Silbury Hill; Sharples 1991, Maiden Castle) refuse scripts or are not online: not used.
National Trust pages (Avebury; White Horse Hill, which answered once and then served a browser check) refuse scripts: not used.
Silbury: the step's height below the summit, and Leary, Field and Campbell 2013 (the full phasing with dimensions) not reached; height disagreement 30 vs 39.3 m to be read from the LiDAR.
Maiden Castle: Sharples 1991 (modern radiocarbon phasing, rampart dimensions) not online; heights of each rampart now from the LiDAR. Wheeler's text is OCR with misreadings.

Uffington: the OSM horse outline looks wrongly oriented (long axis N-S); the OA plan (fig. 5.6) or aerial photographs are needed for the shape. Present widths of the horse's lines (and the 2024 widening) not found in figures.

Avebury Cove: dimensions of the two surviving stones (height, width) not found in a fetchable source; the 2003 Longstones Project report (Gillings et al. 2008, Landscape of the Megaliths) is not online.

Wiltshire Archaeological Magazine (BHL) not searched in depth: older volumes (e.g. Smith 1867 on the 1865 Cove excavation; Cunnington 1913 on the Longstones) could add 19th-century stone descriptions.
